books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Southern Chivalry — Argument versus Club’s (John L. Magee, 1856)
Stephen A. Douglas, Freeport debate answer (August 27, 1858)
John Brown, address to the Virginia court (November 2, 1859)

source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources and real data (see each document’s sourcing note)
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which popular sovereignty failed to settle the question of slavery in the territories in the period 1854–1860.

documents.title: The Kansas-Nebraska Act repeals the Missouri line
documents.source: Kansas-Nebraska Act, “An Act to Organize the Territories of Nebraska and Kansas,” approved May 30, 1854. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Congress, repealing the Missouri Compromise’s ban on slavery north of 36°30′ and handing the question to the settlers.
documents.text: . . . except the eighth section of the act preparatory to the admission of Missouri into the Union, approved March sixth, eighteen hundred and twenty, which, being inconsistent with the principle of non-intervention by Congress with slavery in the States and Territories, as recognized by the legislation of eighteen hundred and fifty, commonly called the Compromise Measures, is hereby declared inoperative and void

documents.title: Sumner: the crime against Kansas
documents.source: Charles Sumner, “The Crime Against Kansas,” speech in the Senate, May 19–20, 1856. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Sumner, the Massachusetts senator, denouncing the proslavery drive to make Kansas a slave state.
documents.text: It is the rape of a virgin Territory, compelling it to the hateful embrace of Slavery; and it may be clearly traced to a depraved longing for a new slave State, the hideous offspring of such a crime, in the hope of adding to the power of Slavery in the National Government.

documents.title: Southern Chivalry: argument versus clubs
documents.source: Southern Chivalry — Argument versus Club’s (John L. Magee, lithograph, 1856). Smithsonian, National Museum of American History. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Magee, a Northern lithographer, mocking Brooks’s beating of Sumner as the South’s answer to debate.

documents.title: The Lecompton Constitution protects slave property
documents.source: Lecompton Constitution, Article VII, Section 1 (1857). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The proslavery convention at Lecompton, writing a constitution for Kansas that puts slave property beyond the voters’ reach.
documents.text: The right of property is before and higher than any constitutional sanction, and the right of the owner of a slave to such slave and its increase is the same and as inviolable as the right of the owner of any property whatever.

documents.title: Douglas: the Freeport Doctrine
documents.source: Stephen A. Douglas, answer at the Freeport debate, August 27, 1858. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Douglas, pressed by Lincoln at Freeport, explaining how a territory could keep slavery out after Dred Scott.
documents.text: It matters not what way the Supreme Court may hereafter decide as to the abstract question whether slavery may or may not go into a Territory under the Constitution, the people have the lawful means to introduce it or exclude it as they please, for the reason that slavery cannot exist a day or an hour anywhere, unless it is supported by local police regulations.

documents.title: John Brown answers the court
documents.source: John Brown, address to the Virginia court, November 2, 1859. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Brown, sentenced to hang for the Harpers Ferry raid, telling the court what he meant to do and why it was right.
documents.text: I never did intend murder, or treason, or the destruction of property, or to excite or incite slaves to rebellion, or to make insurrection. . . . I believe that to have interfered as I have done . . . in behalf of His despised poor, was not wrong, but right.

documents.title: Kansas votes, 1855–1861
documents.source: Kansas territorial votes: Barron’s Premium 2027, Chapter 7, Topic 5.6 (1855 election); English Bill referendum figures, August 2, 1858 (11,300 to 1,788); Kansas admission, January 29, 1861.
documents.sourcing: The record of Kansas votes, showing fraud, a rigged referendum, and a free state at last.
documents.text:
| Vote | Result |
| March 30, 1855, first territorial legislature election | 2,905 eligible voters (territorial census); 6,307 ballots cast |
| August 2, 1858, referendum on the English Bill | 11,300 votes against the Lecompton Constitution, 1,788 for it |
| January 29, 1861 | Kansas admitted to the Union as a free state |

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which popular sovereignty failed, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the Compromise of 1850, the collapse of the Whig Party, or the rise of the Republican Party.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument, or background from a later century, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument about the prompt.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without describing what they show, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument, with the evidence accurately described and tied to the claim.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the Dred Scott decision, the election of 1856, the Lincoln-Douglas debates, or the Panic of 1857.
rubric.notEarned: A general statement with no specific example beyond the documents does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document’s author, purpose, audience, or historical situation to the argument, for at least two documents.
rubric.notEarned: Identifying an author without explaining why it matters, or sourcing only one document, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the extent of the claim, showing how the same development pulled in opposite directions, or weighing change against continuity.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: Popular sovereignty failed to a great extent as a settlement for slavery in the territories, because it moved the fight from Congress to the frontier, where fraud and violence decided what ballots could not.
Grouping 1 — the promise: the Kansas-Nebraska Act (Doc 1) repeals the Missouri line and promises the settlers a free choice.
Grouping 2 — the promise breaks in Kansas: Sumner (Doc 2) denounces the fraud, the Magee cartoon (Doc 3) shows debate answered with a club, and the Kansas votes (Doc 7) record 6,307 ballots from 2,905 eligible voters.
Grouping 3 — the promise breaks in law: the Lecompton Constitution (Doc 4) locks slavery beyond the voters’ reach, Douglas (Doc 5) can only offer unfriendly legislation as a way around the Court, and Brown (Doc 6) answers failure with a raid.
Outside evidence: the Dred Scott decision, the election of 1856, and the Lincoln-Douglas debates.
Complexity: popular sovereignty failed as a settlement, yet it succeeded as a political weapon, since Douglas used it to build a railroad bill and Lincoln used its failure to build a party.
